[PATH:empirical] Panel data on local labor markets from U.S. Census Bureau (e.g., Quarterly Workforce Indicators) and Bureau of Labor Statistics (e.g., OES wage data) linked to housing supply elasticity estimates (e.g., Saiz, 2010). — A difference-in-differences design comparing tech hubs with restrictive vs. elastic housing supply before and during a tech downturn can directly test whether secondary migrant service workers experience steeper real wage declines.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling: A search-and-matching labor market model with endogenous location choice and housing supply constraints (e.g., Diamond, 2016; Notowidigdo, 2013). — A calibrated model can isolate the mechanism: during a tech downturn, low-skilled workers move to tech hubs for service jobs, but restrictive housing supply raises rents and slows demand adjustment, amplifying wage declines. This provides a counterfactual to empirical findings.

[PATH:literature] Literature review: Studies on 'secondary migration' in recessions (e.g., Bound & Holzer, 2000; Cadena & Kovak, 2016) and housing supply effects on local labor markets (e.g., Glaeser & Gyourko, 2005; Saks, 2008). — Synthesizing existing evidence on migration responses to local shocks and housing supply rigidity can assess whether the hypothesized amplification effect is consistent with prior findings or requires new data.

scope.domain: labor economics during recessionary tech cycles with housing supply constraints
